results.title: If you're not Hindu, you're looking through the door
results.text: So, the Shiva art on the outside is interesting, but you're basically looking at the backside of a big brass cow, since non-Hindus can't go inside. The larger world heritage site is pretty interesting, including the cremations along the (filthy) river, smaller shrines, sadhus-for-pay, etc., but the temple itself is unavailable. The pagoda architecture is worth noting, and the people-watching is good, but between the large number of (sacred) cows and their manure, the pigeons, and the cremations and the unshod feet, be prepared for olfactory overload.

results.title: Nepal offers several exciting place to visit.
results.text:
"We were a bunch of four college friend and visited the country some two years back. We friends had been to some other destinations like Dubai and London but this country has some unique things to offer.
The temple was the best among the entire place we paid a visit to. We were initially reluctant to visit the place but our guide was so much informative that he gave us information about the importance of the place. There were a great number of visitors and tourists. We took over hundred pics and all were of different items. I recommend the visitors to spend at least two to four hours at this temple. We were a bit unfortunate to visit this place thoroughly as we were running of time. Some stalls were also set up which were selling historical items related to the temple."

results.title: Holiest of the Holy Temple in Nepal
results.text: A world heritage site - only Hindus can visit from inside - a very powerful place dedicated to specifically lord Shiva - but Also home to all our Gods - clean well kept - ideal to visit early morning

results.title: Very interesting
results.text: Interesting to see the cremation ritual and the site itself has some very impressive buildings, beware of the guys you try to follow you around and give you information on the site,they ask for $20 US and dont show you the whole area,the one i had also tried to get me to buy necklaces from the numerous touts that patrol the area saying that it was not a lot of money to me!!! if you can ignore these guys and go and look around it is worth the visit.

results.text: Where did the monkeys go? And now they charge $10.00US to get into just one part of the temple (you must be Hindu to enter the main temple) and I'm not sure there is much to see.

results.title: Humanity at it's Finest, Very Moving Place...
results.text: This is a traditional Hindu cremation site. it is confronting and beautiful all at the same time. It is not for the faint of heart as multiple funeral pyres burn simultaneously incinerating recently passed Hindu locals. It is a must do in Kathmandu and an excellent opportunity to learn about the Hindu culture.

results.title: Interesting place but really expensive!
results.text:
This holy Hindu place worths the visit if you've never been in India, especially in Varasni.

However, I was mostly disappointed because:
- the site is far less impressive than Varasni
- many tounts, false saddhus.
- when we arrive at cashier, a friendly guy starts to ''show us the way'' of the site. After a few mins, we realised he was a guide. We didn't want any and he wouldn't take no for an answer so it takes a long time to get rid of him. We were then harassed by a lot of ''guides'', something that can really spoil your visit...
- most of all, they have doubled the fee entrance recently (from 500 to 1000rs) without any clear reason. We later learnt by local people that the money isn't used for the improvement of the site - something you can clearly notice during your tour.
Too bad.

results.title: Grim but interesting
results.text:
There happened to be a lot of burning going on when we went, so the acrid smell in the air was off putting, however it is an interesting place. Not too many tourists as well which was surprising.
The cost is the most disappointing part. 1000 rupees despite what the guide book says. The architecture is fascinating as is the ritual.

results.title: overwhelming and beautiful

results.title: Bit of surreal experience
results.text: I visited Pashupatinath about a month ago whilst visiting Kathmandu. I spent most of the time trying to convince people that I was of Indian origin to avoid being swindled out of entrance fees. My attempt as Hindi was okay but not convincing so I opted to speak Punjabi in an attempt to confuse and convince all the same time. It worked and I was allowed into the main area reserved for Hindus only. Once inside, I was greeted by a persistent priest who tried to sell me a pooja (prayer) for 5000 NPR! Once I shooed him away, looking around the main religious area was difficult as people viewed me with suspicious looks of 'is she or she not indian". Although amusing, it somewhat took away my experience of this place as although not religious I have a general interest in these things. That aside, the open air cremations were not as ghastly as I thought they would be, though I hastily retreated when the smoke got too much. Animals roamed everywhere. As you enter, there are lots of cows being constantly fed along with hundreds of pigeons. Beware of the monkeys as they are cheeky but make great photos. Bit of surreal place, lots of sadhus and priests trying to rip you off, animals and humans trying to coexist in some strange way. Worth going just for the experience and fascination of seeing life and death at the same time.

results.title: Sensory overload
results.text:
Bodies burning, funeral music blaring from tinny loudspeakers, hawkers, hustlers and beggars, feral dogs, angry monkeys, holy (oh yeah?) men daubed in ash and paint demanding money to pose for a photo... to the westerner this has to be one of the weirdest places on Earth.

It's worth a visit out of macabre fascination, even though you will feel ripped off by the graveside. But if you think Pashupatinath is a normal, traditional Nepali scene don't kid yourself. Apparently the Nepalese who send off their deceased in the holy river think it is just as tacky as we do, and they want the excessive trappings of tourism driven from this place. You can't blame them.
